query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Doping the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with controlled amounts of boron and nitrogen to enable the in situ generation of a thin, high‐temperature stable hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) tribofilm during sliding will lower friction and wear across the entire 25–800 °C range relative to the undoped alloy.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor doping of boron and nitrogen into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests conducted in ambient air at temperatures ranging from room temperature (approximately 25 °C) up to 800 °C under comparable load conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formed, continuous hBN tribolayer that develops on the wear surface.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the introduced B and N react via tribo-oxidation to produce a self-healing hBN layer that is known for its lubricious nature and thermal stability. This protective film reduces direct metal-to-metal interaction and mitigates adhesive and abrasive wear, maintaining a low friction coefficient and wear rate across the temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The B and N doped alloy will exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate throughout the entire temperature interval, compared with the starting undoped CoCrFeNi material.
generation.baseline: The original CoCrFeNi alloy without B and N doping, which tends to suffer from increased friction and wear especially at elevated temperatures due to unstable or inadequate surface tribolayers.
generation.boundary: Tested under sliding conditions in ambient air at temperatures from roughly 25 °C to 800 °C and under similar load and sliding speed conditions, thereby allowing direct performance comparison across the temperature regime.
generation.uncertainty: The extent and uniformity of hBN layer formation may vary with temperature and sliding dynamics, and the precise magnitude of friction and wear improvement is uncertain; additional factors such as dopant distribution and oxidation kinetics might affect results.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and one set doped with predetermined low levels of boron and nitrogen. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests in ambient air, incrementally heating from room temperature to 800 °C while controlling load and sliding speed. Post-test analysis will include friction force measurements and wear track characterization.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature during sliding.
Wear track depth and volume loss analysis using profilometry or microscopy.
Surface and cross-sectional analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS, Raman spectroscopy) to verify the formation of hBN tribolayers.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the B and N doped samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the undoped baseline, or if hBN is not observed on the worn surface, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
